pages.text: How to Spot the ‘Loneliest Star’ in the Autumn Night Sky | National Geographic SCIENCE NIGHT SKY GUIDE How to Spot the ‘Loneliest Star’ in the Autumn Night Sky Just 25 light-years from Earth, Fomalhaut is surrounded by vast belts of dust that could reveal the gravitational fingerprints of undiscovered worlds. Fomalhaut, one of the brightest stars in the autumn night sky, lies about 25 light-years from Earth. Roughly 15 times as luminous as our sun, the star is surrounded by vast belts of dust that may hold clues to planets astronomers have yet to discover. NASA, ESA, and the Digitized Sky Survey 2 By Stefanie Waldek Published October 23, 2026 On an autumn night in the Northern Hemisphere, Fomalhaut appears as a bright pinprick in a field of darkness, far from other bright stars. But the star’s apparent solitude is only part of its story: It sits at the center of an expansive system of dusty belts that may hold clues to worlds we have yet to find. Fomalhaut’s name comes from the Arabic fam al-ḥūt , meaning “mouth of the fish,” reflecting its place in the constellation Piscis Austrinus, or the Southern Fish. In a tradition attributed to ancient Persia, Fomalhaut is one of four “Royal Stars,” celestial markers associated with the cardinal directions. An “arboreal archaeologist,” Dalla Ragione scours Renaissance paintings and medieval archives, discovering endangered fruits that might be revived. Her life’s work offers a possible solution to the problem of monocrops. Year after year, agricultural giants cultivate the same varieties of the same fruits and vegetables, while many other varieties have fallen to the wayside. Monocrops contribute to climate change and are highly susceptible to its consequences, jeopardizing our food supply. In this episode, Dalla Ragione and Smithsonian contributing writer Mark Schapiro discuss the importance and challenges of protecting biodiversity and agriculture in the midst of a changing climate—and why it matters. pages.text: How uncharted caves in Greenland could predict the Earth's future | National Geographic By Yudhijit Bhattacharjee Photographs by Robbie Shone Published January 8, 2025 The helicopter landed on top of the cliff, its blades chopping the cold air. Stepping out, National Geographic Explorer Gina Moseley breathed deeply and took in the commanding view of Greenland ’s barren landscape. To the south, a frozen lake stretched out for miles, eventually giving way to brown and gray plateaus, interrupted by the white flash of glaciers in the distance. In the other direction, some 560 miles beyond the horizon, was the North Pole. The only other human presence was the helicopter pilot and the other passengers: Moseley’s life partner and this story’s photographer and fellow National Geographic Explorer, Robbie Shone, and technical climbing specialist Chris Blakeley. The weather was mild, just above freezing—perfect, actually—but Moseley knew that storms could blow up at a moment’s notice, bringing dangerous winds and dense fog. In such a case, they’d have to leave immediately or risk being stranded in one of the world’s most remote and forbidding environments. They were poised on the edge separating potential disaster and sublime discovery. For more than a decade, Moseley—a British paleoclimatologist and caver—had envisioned this moment, hoping to be part of the first team to set foot inside the Wulff Land Cave (WUL-8), one of the most isolated caves on Earth. Nearly 30 years ago, a 10-year-old Doran had sat in front of her family's TV, reading out the dialogue on screen to her sister, a year younger, as they inched their way through the original Nintendo 64 game's sprawling, puzzle-filled dungeons. pages.description: While always popular in the Austrian capital, these events have taken off in the digital age, with online platforms drawing a new generation to fairytale dance floors.
pages.text: How Vienna's Ball Scene Has Evolved in the Digital Age | National Geographic TRAVEL How Vienna's Ball Scene Has Evolved in the Digital Age While always popular in the Austrian capital, these events have taken off in the digital age, with online platforms drawing a new generation to fairytale dance floors. The Vienna Philharmonic Ball is held in the Golden Hall of the Musikverein. Paul Bauer, Wien Tourismus By Ellen Himelfarb Published October 12, 2026 This article was produced by National Geographic Traveller (UK). On 11 November, Vienna’s palaces and music halls kick into high gear. Dance floors swarm with couples waltzing in choreographed swirls — and freestyling to live electropop. The two scenes are complementary halves of the Austrian capital’s modern ball scene: an old custom attracting new attention, buoyed by social media and miles of bias-cut silk. The festivities trace their roots to the 1700s, when Emperor Joseph II opened the Hofburg Palace dances — until then, reserved for nobility — to ordinary citizens. The decision paved the way for a wider ball culture to develop in the following centuries. Public dancing venues expanded, professional groups began holding their own balls and the dances became key fixtures in the city’s social calendar — a tradition that continues to this day. When Gen Z came of age, they box-stepped into Ballsaison (ball season) fuelled by a penchant for retro style and, crucially, posting the pageantry online. pages.title: How Wales captain Dewi Lake's rousing speech inspired historic win against All Blacks - BBC Sport
pages.description: Dewi Lake's rousing team talk helped ensure Wales did not let the chance to make history against New Zealand slip away.
pages.text: How Wales captain Dewi Lake's rousing speech inspired historic win against All Blacks - BBC Sport Image source, Huw Evans Picture Agency Image caption, Dewi Lake has captained Wales 24 times Published 16 November 2026 Inside the Wales dressing room at the Principality Stadium at half-time on Saturday, heads could easily have bowed. Visitors New Zealand had just levelled the scores at 21-21 with the clock in the red at the end of the first half. It was a sucker punch that could have knocked the wind out of Welsh sails. But captain Dewi Lake summoned the words that inspired a first win over New Zealand in 73 years. With a rousing speech, the captain reminded his players of the feeling in the same changing room 12 months earlier, when they trailed by just three points at the break only to eventually lose 52-26. "Dewi made a very good point, the last time that we played them we had been in the contest, but let the dam break," Leicester and Wales wing Gabriel Hamer-Webb told the Rugby Union Weekly podcast. "They slipped through and we promised ourselves that we weren't going to let that happen again, that we had an opportunity to really do something special. "The heart the boys showed from then on, we wanted it more than they did. New Zealand were shocked and there was no way that we were going to let it slip." Help for Survey Participants How We Conduct Our Surveys In addition to conducting the decennial census count, the Census Bureau conducts various surveys that study households, businesses, schools, hospitals, and more. The Census Bureau will notify you in advance if you are in a survey, provide different ways to respond, and may follow up with you. We notify you if you are in a survey. The U.S. Census Bureau typically sends an official letter describing the survey for which your household or business has been selected and why your participation is important. This letter describes what the survey is, what type of questions will be asked, and what you can expect as a survey participant. For household surveys, most mailings from the Census Bureau are addressed to “the resident of.” Household surveys from the Census Bureau are only mailed to residential addresses, not to P.O. Boxes. P.O. Boxes are not associated with specific addresses, so the Census Bureau cannot use them as a mailing destination. If you are visited by a field representative working on a survey and have not yet received a survey letter or notice from the Census Bureau, you can request one from the representative at your door. You may also contact the Census Bureau Regional Office for your state for more information. Some surveys send invitations via text message or email. You can verify an email or text message is from the Census Bureau by noting the email address or phone number from which the invitation was sent.

A facsimile of the Trojan Horse in the port city of Çanakkale, Türkiye, draws travelers and fans of the epic Greek poems. dinosmichail, Alamy By Nick Hilden Published July 17, 2026 Driving south out of the petite port town of Çanakkale, on the northwestern tip of Türkiye, signs for “Truva” and “Troya” begin to appear with growing frequency. The bustle of modern life gives way to the pastoral, and half an hour later, you’re in the ancient city of Troy, some 3,000 years in the past. A towering wooden horse greets you at the gate and all around are scattered ruins, the Aegean Sea in the distance, and the plains upon which the legendary Trojan War was fought in between. “The aura is so strong, [that] when Caesar visited Troy he said, ‘Every stone has a name,’” says Rüstem Aslan , a professor at Çanakkale Onsekiz Mart University , who has spent 40 years excavating the UNESCO World Heritage site believed to be the legendary city. Today, Hisarlik—Turkish for “ place of fortresses ,” the name for the hill where the ruins lie—recounts its history through the Troy Museum and the remains of architectural structures containing the echoes of Homer ’s great epic, The Odyssey . HPV vaccination can be started at age 9 years. Introduction HPV vaccination provides safe, effective, and lasting protection against the HPV infections that most commonly cause cancer. The HPV vaccine series is most effective when given before a person is exposed to the virus. Every year in the United States, HPV causes about 36,000 cases of cancer in both men and women. Keep Reading: Reasons to Get Vaccinated Available vaccines There are several types of HPV vaccines. That's why HPV vaccine is recommended earlier rather than later. This vaccine protects against nine HPV types (6, 11, 16, 18, 31, 33, 45, 52, and 58). pages.text: Hull man and wife who fled Ukraine return to a warzone Skip to content Site search Home News Sport Business Technology Health Culture Arts Travel Earth Audio Video Live Documentaries Weather Newsletters Watch Live 'Friends think we're idiots for returning to Ukraine' 21 hours ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Kevin Shoesmith East Yorkshire and Lincolnshire John Holmes Liliya Holmes and her British husband John pictured in Odesa, Ukraine When Russian forces launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, John Holmes – a British national – and his Ukrainian wife Liliya fled the port city of Odesa, fearing for their lives. But after four years in the UK, the draw of home has proven too strong and they have returned to Ukraine's third largest city, undeterred by the sustained threat of air raids. "Friends of ours thought we were idiots for going back to Ukraine," reflects John, 74. "But returning is something we felt we needed to do. "Yes, it's dangerous. Yes, there are drones flying overhead. Yes, you can hear the explosions. But you just have to get on with life as best you can. "Home is Ukraine." During their time away, the pair sought sanctuary in Hull , East Yorkshire, where John was born and raised and has a property. He met Liliya, 64, in Ukraine and had been living there for 30 years until the invasion. "We had built a good life here," he says. pages.text: Human jaws are surprisingly strong and efficient | National Geographic SCIENCE NOT EXACTLY ROCKET SCIENCE Human jaws are surprisingly strong and efficient By Ed Yong Published June 22, 2010 • 4 min read Stephen Wroe has built a career out of analysing some of the planet’s most formidable skulls. His group at the University of New South Wales have studied the strength, sturdiness and biting power of the sabre-toothed cat , the great white shark , and the Komodo dragon . Now, he has turned his attention to a predator whose skull is far less impressive but yields surprises all the same – us. Humans, it is said, have relatively weak jaws that can’t inflict or withstand high bite forces. Some have suggested that we are adapted to eat foods that aren’t very tough, or that our use of tools and cooking has lessened the evolutionary pressure on maintaining sturdy jaws. Some have even suggested that our weedy jaw muscles made way for our large brains and thus facilitated their evolution. But according to Wroe, all of these explanations have a fatal flaw – our jaws aren’t weak at all. They’re actually remarkably efficient for a primate. The notion of weak human chops was based on very unrefined models that treated our jaws as two-dimensional levers. Of course, in real life, we chew in three glorious dimensions. To really understand how strong our mandibles are, we need to add that third dimension to the models. That’s exactly what Wroe did. He used his signature technique, called finite element analysis , to create a virtual model of a human skull (belonging to a San hunter-gatherer).

By Michael Greshko Published April 26, 2017 • 15 min read In an announcement sure to spark a firestorm of controversy, researchers say they’ve found signs of ancient humans in California between 120,000 and 140,000 years ago—more than a hundred thousand years before humans were thought to exist anywhere in the Americas. pages.text: Humans used to have straighter teeth—what changed? | National Geographic HEALTH Humans used to have straighter teeth—what changed? New research explores how diet, evolution, and facial anatomy may have shaped our modern smiles. Studies of ancient skulls show wider jaws and fewer malocclusions, leading researchers to explore how diet and lifestyle shaped the human face. Photograph by Alan/Adobe Stock By Leah Worthington Published July 15, 2025 Braces, rubber bands, even jaw surgery—millions endure them in pursuit of a straighter smile. But were misaligned smiles always this common? Research suggests that might not be the case. While malocclusions—crowded or misaligned teeth—have been found among our hunter-gatherer ancestors, they appear to be more prevalent in modern populations. So what changed? Experts say the answer isn’t simple but point to one possible culprit: our diets. As we traded raw, tough foods for softer, more processed ones, the burden of chewing decreased, allowing our jaws to shrink over time. Now, researchers are exploring how evolutionary biology, diet, and modern lifestyles may have reshaped our faces—and our smiles. How farming may have reshaped the human face Ancient human skulls were strikingly different from our own. Early hunter-gatherers had large, powerful jaws built for the demanding work of chewing tough meats, fibrous vegetables, seeds, and nuts. But around 12,000 years ago, things began to change. pages.text: Hundreds still homeless after 'unsafe' Canning Town flats evacuation Skip to content Site search Home News Sport Business Technology Health Culture Arts Travel Earth Audio Video Live Documentaries Weather Newsletters Watch Live Hundreds still homeless after being evacuated from 'unsafe' flats 4 hours ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Ayshea Buksh London BBC The Royal Gateway, also known as Caxton Works, was advertised as "an exciting regeneration project" when it was built Hundreds of residents in east London remain homeless after structural defects were discovered at an award-winning high-rise development that was declared "at risk of sudden collapse". The Royal Gateway, also known as Caxton Works in Canning Town, Newham, was built less than 10 years ago. But last month, people living there were suddenly told to leave - some in the middle of the night by London Fire Brigade - because it was "unsafe". Businesses renting commercial spaces were also told to evacuate their premises. Engineers identified concerns with reinforced concrete "transfer slabs" supporting the buildings - an issue that has emerged at other London developments, prompting wider scrutiny of the construction method. Property company Galliard Homes, which built the scheme, says it is working to "investigate the concerns and develop potential solutions", while giving financial and practical support to residents. pages.text: Hungary v Northern Ireland: We want to play on the biggest stages - Isaac Price - BBC Sport Image source, Press Eye Image caption, West Brom midfielder Isaac Price has started Northern Ireland's last 25 matches By Andy Gray BBC Sport NI Journalist Published 16 November 2026 When Northern Ireland step out into the Puskas Arena on Tuesday night, they hope it will be a taste of what is to come. In the 70,000-seater stadium, which hosted the Champions League final between Paris St-Germain and Arsenal in May, Northern Ireland's destiny will be in their own hands. In 18 months' time, Michael O'Neill's young side will hope be at the Euro 2028 finals. But for now, they face Hungary with hopes of promotion to League A in the Nations League for the first time. A win or a draw will do the job in Budapest, and it would be the latest step for a Northern Ireland side who continue to show encouraging signs in their development. Worst case, NI will still have a shot at a play-off for League A in March but their sole aim is to get the job done on Tuesday. Midfielder Isaac Price, who has grown into a key player under O'Neill, says you "have got to love the expectation". "That's what you play football for. We're playing in a stadium where 70,000 people will be watching and then there'll be loads more at home watching," he told BBC Sport NI. "That's what you grow up and want to do. The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping is the sixth movie in the franchise, and tells the origin story of a teenage Haymitch Abernathy - who was played as an adult by Woody Harrelson. In a one-star review, the Guardian called the film "overwrought and boring", and said it "has no actual interest and no authentic reason to exist, other than to gouge an income stream out of its fanbase". But the Wrap praised its "memorable performances, intoxicating style and horrifying commentary", adding: "When the dust settles it may even be the Hunger Games that holds up best." In a closing speech, prosecutor Christopher Paxton KC told Cambridge Crown Court Williams had "deadly intention", adding: "The fists and feet of this big powerful man as he was described were not weapons enough." Williams, 33, of Langford Road, Peterborough, also denies four counts of attempted murder in relation to earlier attacks in his home city and London. Jurors have seen CCTV footage of Williams' attack on board the LNER train, which allegedly began between Peterborough and Stevenage. Paxton began his speech by repeating some of the words jurors have heard Williams said. "I've got a knife and I'm not afraid to use it. You're all going to die today. Do you want to die? Hydraulic Properties The Office of Geothermal’s Innovative Methods to Control Hydraulic Properties of Enhanced Geothermal Systems (EGS) , or Hydraulic Properties, initiative supports the research, development, demonstration, and deployment of technologies and techniques to control the fluid flow within the fracture network in EGS reservoirs in order to optimize them for heat extraction. EGS systems use human-made reservoirs to access subsurface heat where natural subsurface conditions lack sufficient fluid flow—or permeability—or water to allow heat to be drawn to the surface for energy. Projects under this initiative are developing targeted and reversible in-reservoir fracture permeability modification systems or methods and yield long-term reservoir productivity improvements. The ability to customize reservoirs via these methods will increase reservoir efficiency and longevity, ultimately helping to drive down EGS costs, reduce the risk of development, and accelerate the path towards widespread commercialization. Hydrothermal Resources What Are Hydrothermal Resources? The natural formation of a hydrothermal resource requires three principal elements: heat, water, and permeability. When water is heated in the earth, hot water or steam is trapped in porous and fractured rocks beneath a layer of relatively impermeable caprock, resulting in the formation of a hydrothermal reservoir. If the conditions underground are right, humans can harness that geothermal hot water or steam by drilling and then bring it to the surface to generate electricity . These types of geothermal systems typically occur close to tectonic plate boundaries, like in the western portions of the United States. Sometimes the resource is easy to find because of indicators on the surface like hot springs. Other times, conventional geothermal resources are “ hidden ,” with no signs of the underground reservoir on the surface. Hydrothermal resources are considered conventional geothermal resources because they can be developed using existing technologies and do not require creation of human-made reservoirs as needed with enhanced geothermal systems . Practicing good hygiene is a core prevention strategy recommended for everyone to lower your risks from respiratory illnesses. Recommendation Practice good hygiene by covering your coughs and sneezes, washing or sanitizing your hands often, and cleaning frequently touched surfaces. How it works Covering your coughs and sneezes limits the spread of germs to protect others. Handwashing with soap removes germs from your hands, making them less likely to infect your respiratory system when you touch your eyes, nose, or mouth. If soap and water are not available, using a hand sanitizer with at least 60 percent alcohol can kill these germs. To remove germs and dirt on surfaces, use household cleaners that contain soap or detergent. Steps you can take Cover your mouth and nose with a tissue when you cough or sneeze . But I felt nothing. I did not cry, nor struggle to sleep. I seldom thought of him. I felt only guilt about how little I felt. Ours was a complex relationship. As a teen, I often resented my dad, occasionally despised him. I expected the world and found disappointment. But, as I grew older, I understood that he had struggles of his own. I learned to appreciate his decency and humour, his ability to make everyone laugh with only a few words. I loved my dad, from the first time he held me to the last time I held him. But still, as weeks turned into months, I struggled to grieve. Then, when my partner and I rearranged our bookshelves, I found the first edition of Under Milk Wood that my parents gave us on our wedding day. I turned the cover and saw the note: “And all the bells of the tills of the town shall ring for our wedding.” It was my mum’s writing, but my dad’s idea.

Cancer treatment and your blood sugar Chemotherapy , or chemo, helps kill or shrink cancer cells, but it also hurts some healthy cells.
